subskill: form: singular finite verb after a singular head separated from it by an "including" phrase ending in plural nouns, crossed with active vs passive voice (object delayed past a parenthetical)
passage: Harbor walls built by Roman engineers have stood in seawater for two thousand years, while many modern concrete piers crumble within decades. The difference may lie in how the ancient material repairs itself. The mortar in these walls, including its white lumps of lime and its glassy volcanic fragments, ______, a team of materials scientists has argued, the hairline cracks that seawater opens: as water seeps in, the lime dissolves and recrystallizes as calcite inside each crack.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject of the verb is the singular noun "The mortar"; the phrase "including its white lumps of lime and its glassy volcanic fragments" is set off by commas and does not change the subject's number, so the verb must be singular. The verb must also be active, because the mortar does something to an object: after the parenthetical "a team of materials scientists has argued," the clause continues with "the hairline cracks that seawater opens," which is the direct object. "repeatedly seals" is singular and active, so it is correct. "repeatedly seal" is active but plural; it agrees with "fragments" rather than with "The mortar." "is repeatedly sealed" is singular but passive, which leaves "the hairline cracks" with no grammatical role in the clause. "are repeatedly sealed" is both plural and passive.
template: singular head + comma-set "including" phrase ending in plural noun x plural attractor next to the blank x number by voice (present active / present passive), object delayed by a parenthetical

subskill: form: singular verb after a fraction + "of" + singular mass noun (partitive agreement with the nearest noun), with earlier plural attractors, crossed with active vs passive voice
passage: Coastal salt marshes are often praised as carbon sinks, and the credit usually goes to their dense stands of cordgrass. But when ecologists analyzed the chemical signatures of sediment cores from a dozen marshes along the Atlantic coast, they found that in most of the cores roughly two-thirds of the buried carbon ______ into the marsh from elsewhere, carried in on the tides as fine particles of seaweed and river-borne plant debris. The grasses, it seems, mainly act as a filter.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: With a fraction such as "two-thirds of," the verb agrees with the noun after "of." Here that noun is "carbon," a singular mass noun, so the verb must be singular even though "two-thirds" sounds plural and the sentence is crowded with plural nouns ("cores," "marshes," "signatures"). The verb must also be passive: the carbon does not bring anything; it was carried into the marsh by the tides, and nothing in the rest of the clause ("into the marsh from elsewhere, carried in on the tides...") can serve as an object for an active "bring." "was actually brought" is singular and passive, so it is correct. "were actually brought" is passive but plural, agreeing with "two-thirds" or "cores" instead of "carbon." "had actually brought" is active, so it would make the carbon the bringer of something, and the clause supplies no object. "actually brought" can only be read as active past (again with no object) or as a participle modifying "carbon," which would leave the clause after "found that" with no main verb at all.
topic_tag: coastal biogeochemistry: salt marsh carbon sources
template: fraction + of + singular mass noun right before the blank (nearest noun AGREES) x plural fraction feel and earlier plural attractors x number by voice (past passive / past active / bare participle)

subskill: form: plural verb after a plural subject followed by floating "each" (subject head far from the blank), crossed with progressive passive vs progressive active voice
passage: A folklorist spent two summers in a remote mountain valley writing down ballads that farm families had sung for generations, often recording several versions of a single song. The two notebooks in which she transcribed the families' ballads each ______ at a separate library, one near the valley and one in a distant capital, where volunteers photograph a few pages every week. Until that work is finished, a scholar who wants to compare her versions line by line must travel between them.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject is "The two notebooks," which is plural. When "each" follows a plural subject rather than serving as the subject itself, it does not make the verb singular: "The two notebooks ... each are," not "each is." The verb must also be passive. The notebooks are not doing the digitizing; the passage names who is ("volunteers photograph a few pages every week"), and nothing in the clause after the blank ("at a separate library, one near the valley and one in a distant capital") can serve as the object an active "digitizing" requires. "are now being digitized" is plural and passive, so it is correct. "is now being digitized" is passive but singular, treating "each" as the subject. "are now digitizing" is plural but active, making the notebooks the ones digitizing something with no object. "is now digitizing" is both singular and active.
template: plural subject + relative clause + floating "each" (noun before each AGREES) x "each" tempting singular x number by voice in the present progressive (are/is being + participle vs are/is + -ing), agent named in a later clause

subskill: form: nonfinite (present participle) result phrase required after a complete clause and a comma; finite options create a second predicate joined by a comma alone, crossed with participle aspect (simple vs perfect)
passage: Large rivers crossing flat deltas rarely stay in one bed for long. Over centuries, sediment settles in a river's channel until the riverbed sits higher than the surrounding floodplain; then, during a major flood, the water breaks through a bank and carves a new route to the sea, ______ along the abandoned channel without the waterway that once carried their trade.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The clause "the water breaks through a bank and carves a new route to the sea" is already complete, and only a comma follows it, so the blank must begin a modifying phrase rather than a new verb of the same subject. A present participle phrase does this and expresses the result of the flood: "leaving riverside towns along the abandoned channel without the waterway." "left riverside towns" and "had left riverside towns" are finite verbs; each would add a third predicate to "breaks ... and carves" with only a comma and no conjunction, and their past tenses also clash with the present tense "breaks" and "carves." "having left riverside towns" is nonfinite, but the perfect participle places the leaving before the main action, which is illogical: the towns are stranded as a result of the new route, not before it.
template: complete present-tense clause + comma + blank x finite verbs tempting a compound predicate x nonfinite vs finite by aspect/tense (present participle / perfect participle / simple past / past perfect)

subskill: form: future-in-the-past ("would" + base) after a past reporting verb when the predicted event lies in the narrative past, decided by later sentences showing the prediction failed
passage: The engineer hired by a small fishing town to design a stone breakwater for its harbor assured the council that the new wall ______ the sand carried along the coast by winter currents. The opposite occurred. Once built, the breakwater created a pocket of calm water where sand settled faster than ever, and within a few years the town was paying dredging crews every spring to keep the channel open.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The engineer's assurance is reported with a past-tense verb, "assured," and it concerned something that, from the time of the assurance, still lay ahead: the wall had not yet been built ("hired ... to design"). A future seen from a past point is expressed with "would" plus the base verb. The later sentences confirm that the whole episode is in the past and that the prediction has already been tested and failed ("The opposite occurred," "the town was paying dredging crews"), so "would keep out" is correct. "will keep out" speaks from the present about a still-open future, which contradicts the narrative showing the outcome is already known. "keeps out" uses the present tense for an event that, at the time of the assurance, had not happened. "had kept out" places the keeping out before the assurance, when the wall did not yet exist.
template: past reporting verb ("assured that") + predicted event x "will" tempting because it is a prediction x future-in-past by tense (would + base / will + base / present / past perfect), decided by later sentences

subskill: form: passive modal ("can be determined") required because the singular subject is the thing acted upon and the clause has no object, crossed with tense consistency against a past perfect passive
passage: Charred cereal grains are among the most valuable finds at early farming sites. Burning turns a grain into carbon that resists decay, so it survives in the soil for thousands of years, and because each grain grew in a single season, the age of even one seed ______ with remarkable precision from a fragment smaller than a speck of dust, allowing archaeologists to date the very first harvests at a site.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject, "the age of even one seed," is the thing that is measured, not the thing doing the measuring, and the rest of the clause ("with remarkable precision from a fragment smaller than a speck of dust") contains no object for an active verb. The verb must therefore be passive. The passage describes what is generally true now ("are among," "turns," "survives"), so a present modal fits: "can be determined." "can determine" is active, making the age the one that determines something and leaving the verb without an object. "has determined" is likewise active and objectless. "had been determined" is passive but past perfect, which requires an earlier past reference point; the passage is set in the general present, so it does not fit.
template: singular abstract subject acted upon ("the age of ... seed") x active modal tempting, no object x voice by modal/perfect (modal active / perfect active / past perfect passive / modal passive)

subskill: boundaries: colon after an independent clause to introduce a single noun-phrase explanation; semicolon creates a fragment, comma makes the phrase rename the wrong noun
passage: Typefaces drawn for telephone directories had to stay legible at small sizes on thin, absorbent paper fed through high-speed presses. Under those conditions, ink pooled wherever two strokes met at a sharp angle, blotting letters into smudges. One designer countered the problem with a feature that is invisible at normal reading distance yet obvious under ______ notches at each such junction that give the excess ink room to spread without blurring the letter.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The words before the blank form a complete independent clause that announces something ("One designer countered the problem with a feature that is invisible at normal reading distance yet obvious under magnification"), and the words after it identify that feature: "deep notches at each such junction that give the excess ink room to spread." A colon is the mark that introduces such an explanation, so "magnification: deep" is correct. "magnification; deep" is wrong because a semicolon must join two independent clauses, and "deep notches at each such junction ..." has no main verb ("give" belongs to the relative clause "that give"). "magnification, deep" makes the noun phrase an appositive renaming "magnification," which is illogical: the notches are the feature, not the magnification. "magnification deep" runs the two noun phrases together with no punctuation, producing an ungrammatical string.
template: independent clause ending in a noun that is NOT the thing explained + blank + single noun phrase with relative clause x comma tempting as appositive x colon/semicolon/comma/no mark (identical words), colon key

subskill: boundaries: dash after a fronted list of noun phrases, resumed by a summarizing subject; period leaves the list as a fragment sentence
passage: Bodies recovered from northern European peat bogs can retain skin, hair, and even the contents of the stomach after two thousand years. Botanists credit the bog itself, and in particular the sphagnum moss that forms it. Cold water, acid released by the moss, and an almost complete absence of ______ one of these conditions would slow the bacteria that break down soft tissue. Together, they halt decay almost entirely.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The sentence opens with a list of three noun phrases ("Cold water, acid released by the moss, and an almost complete absence of oxygen") that has no verb of its own; the main clause is "any one of these conditions would slow the bacteria," whose subject sums up the list. A dash is the mark that sets a fronted list off from a clause that resumes it, so "oxygen—any" is correct. "oxygen. Any" is wrong because the period would end a sentence consisting only of the list, which has no verb and is therefore a fragment. "oxygen, any" leaves the list dangling, attached to the clause by a comma with no grammatical role, since the clause already has its own subject ("any one of these conditions"). "oxygen any" runs the list straight into the clause with no punctuation, which is ungrammatical.
topic_tag: bog preservation: sphagnum and soft tissue
template: fronted verbless list of noun phrases + blank + resumptive subject clause x period tempting as a strong break x dash/period/comma/no mark (identical words), dash key
